cargo is the reason Rust projects are pleasant to work in. It is a build system, dependency manager, test runner, doc generator and release tool, and it is the only one you need.

Create a project

That compile time is the entire crate. Your first real project will take longer because it compiles dependencies — once. Incremental builds after that are fast.

The five commands you will type forever

Command What it does When
cargo check Type-checks without producing a binary While writing code — 2–5× faster than build
cargo build Compiles to target/debug/ Before running
cargo run build then execute Iterating
cargo test Builds and runs tests Constantly
cargo build --release Optimised build to target/release/ Shipping, benchmarking

Rule of thumb: bind cargo check to a keyboard shortcut in your editor. You will run it hundreds of times a day. It skips code generation and linking, which is most of the time on incremental builds.

Debug vs release

dev (default) release
Optimisation opt-level = 0 opt-level = 3
Debug symbols yes no
Integer overflow panics wraps silently
debug_assert! runs compiled out
Speed 10–100× slower baseline

Gotcha: integer overflow panics in debug and wraps in release. A test that passes in cargo test can behave differently in production. Use checked_add, saturating_add or wrapping_add when the boundary matters.

A real first program

Enough ceremony. Here is something with actual logic: a word-frequency counter, which touches files, HashMap, iterators and error handling.

Things worth noticing, because each becomes a whole module later:

  • env::args().nth(1) returns Option<String> — no null, no exception.
  • fs::read_to_string returns Result<String, io::Error> — failure is a value.
  • counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) — the entry API, which avoids a double lookup.
  • &str keys borrowed from text — the map borrows instead of copying (module 02.03).
  • ExitCode instead of std::process::exit — destructors still run.
  • println!("{n:>5} {word}") — inline format args, right-aligned width 5.

Cargo.toml explained

Version requirements are not exact versions

Cargo picks the newest version satisfying all constraints in the graph and records the result in Cargo.lock. Commit Cargo.lock for binaries (reproducible builds) — it is optional for libraries but increasingly committed anyway.

Adding dependencies

cargo add resolves the latest compatible version, checks features exist, and writes the correct line. It is strictly better than hand-editing Cargo.toml.

Inspect what you actually got:

Gotcha: cargo tree -d showing a crate twice at different major versions is normal (rand 0.8 + rand 0.9) and mostly harmless. It becomes a problem when the type appears in your public API, because then your users cannot pass their version to you.

Your first library crate

Two tests ran from one file: the unit test, and the doc test compiled from the example in the doc comment. That is why Rust docs do not rot — the examples in them are executed by CI.

cargo doc --open now renders greeting with that example inlined and runnable.

Exercises

  1. Extend the word counter: accept multiple files, aggregate counts across all of them, and skip words shorter than 3 characters.
  2. Add --top N support using env::args(). What happens with a non-numeric argument? Decide: panic or error message? Justify your choice.
  3. Make greet a library with a binary that uses it. You will need both src/lib.rs and src/main.rs in one package. Does use greet::greeting; work from main.rs? (It should.)
  4. Run cargo tree on any project. Find one crate that appears at two different versions and explain why.
